parts.why: Check B box 1: the picture is a jar with a cloth lid; a child says 'jar' or 'jam' (1 syllable), not 'honey' (2), so the key marks a correct count wrong. Replace it with a picture that has one name (apple, tiger, pencil). Also both forms have the same answers in the same order (2, 3, 1); change the order in one form.

Check A box 1: the picture shows two birds sitting in a nest; many children will say 'birds' and write B, and the key says N. Replace it with one clear object that starts with a single consonant (net, nut, nose). Check B (tie, fox, hand) is clean, so A is the harder form as it stands.

All four words are too hard for Kindergarten: camel and koala have 5 sounds and 2 syllables, wolf and swan have 4 sounds with a blend; Kindergarten segments 2- and 3-sound words (CVC). 'Camel' is also said 'cam-l' (4 sounds) by many children. Use words of 2 or 3 sounds (for example A: bee, pig; B: cow, hen), and do not give both forms the same answers in the same order (now 5, 4 and 5, 4).

Check B box 2 'tiger': the key wants t-i-g-er (er in one box), but r-controlled vowels are not in this unit and a child who writes t-i-g-e-r in five boxes has a good defense; Check A box 1 'zebra' ends in a schwa that children write as u. The forms also do not match: A has 5 sounds + 3 sounds with a digraph, B has 4 + 4 with no digraph. Use regular words in both forms: one 4-sound word with a blend (frog, crab, drum) and one 3-sound word with sh/ch/th (fish, ship, moth).

horse, camel, apple and lemon all have a part a first grader cannot hear (silent e, -le, a schwa spelled e or o); first graders spell untaught words by sound (hors, caml, apl, lemin), so with one point only for a completely right word almost every child scores 0 on both forms. Use words that are spelled the way they sound (A: frog, crab; B: drum, plum) or tell the teacher in the key to accept spellings that show every sound.

Check A box 2 'Lily draws the vulture.': a first grader cannot read 'vulture' and most do not know the word; use a word they can read (Lily draws the cat / the bus). In all four boxes the small picture also works against the sentence (a chef cooking for 'at the pool', a man in a lab coat standing up for 'in bed'): remove the pictures or use a plain child portrait.

Check A box 1 (answer / reply / question) is far above Grade 1 reading and much harder than Check B (good / bad, bright / dark), so the after-check is the easier form; replace it with a pair at the level of B (for example hot: warm, cold, big). Check B box 1: 'slow' can also be defended as the opposite of 'bright' (a bright child, a slow child); replace 'slow' with a word that has nothing to do with bright (for example 'wet').

Check A box 1 prints the word 'hen' under the picture; the other three boxes print no word. So one box is copy-and-add-s and the others are not, and without a label the birds in box 1 would be 'chickens'. Print the singular word under the pictures in all four boxes (hen, duck, bat, ball) or in none (then replace the hens).

Both forms, answer key: the key only outlines the two names and the words He and She; no lines are drawn, so it does not show the answer. Draw the lines (A: He to Oliver, She to Naomi; B: He to Elijah, She to Sofia). The task itself is right and has one answer.

Check B box 1: 'What time does Emma eat?' is as right as the key's 'When does Emma eat?'; the key must list both. Check A box 1: replace 'vulture' with a common word (Ben likes the puppy); with a vulture some children will write 'Who does Ben like?' or 'Which bird does Ben like?'.

In both forms the answers run in counting-down order (A: 7, 6, 5; B: 8, 4, 3), and A has three shapes with many sides while B has two easy ones (4 and 3), so B is clearly easier. Give each form one shape with 3 or 4 sides, one with 5 or 6 and one with 7 or 8, not in order (for example A: 5, 8, 4 and B: 6, 3, 7).

Check A has three pieces (the child must draw two lines), Check B has two pieces (one line): B is clearly easier. Use a two-piece puzzle in both forms, or a three-piece puzzle in both. In the key the answer lines are the same green as the outline; draw them in orange, and make sure they are not printed on the child's page.

Check B: the fox sits facing the front and is almost the same on both sides; only the tail tells the mirror picture from the copy, which a Kindergartner cannot see at this size (on the sheet it was too small for me to check the key). Check A's horse is seen from the side and is clear. Replace the fox with an animal seen from the side (duck, fish, dog).

Answer key, both forms: no lines are drawn; the empty boxes show stray numbers instead (1 and 2 in A, 7 and 8 in B). In Check B the listed answer (C then B) looks reversed: the first empty box needs the nectarine (2nd choice) and the second empty box needs the kiwi (3rd choice). Draw the lines in the key and check B's key against that. The task itself is right, one answer each.

Answer key, both forms: the two answer boxes are outlined but empty; print 69 (A) and 95 (B). The lesson is 'Add and subtract vertically' but both forms only add, and neither needs regrouping; add a second box per form with vertical subtraction, and let one box per form need regrouping (for example 38 + 47 and 62 - 28).

Check A: in '__ x 5 = 25' the missing factor is the same as the printed factor, so a child who just copies the 5 is right, and 5 x 5 is easier than Check B's 4 x 6. Use a fact with two different factors at the level of B (for example __ x 4 = 20 or __ x 6 = 18).

Check A box 1 uses 5 (2 + 2 + 1), Check B box 1 uses 13 (6 + 6 + 1): A is far easier and 5 is below Grade 2. Use an odd number from 11 to 19 in A too (for example 11 or 15). In Check A box 2 the 14 dots are printed as two rows of 7, which shows the answer; print them in uneven rows as in Check B.

instruction.now: Write how many syllables you hear in each word.
instruction.better: I will say the name of each picture. Clap the word. Write how many syllables you hear.
instruction.why: No word is printed, so the count depends on the word the child picks (ladybug or bug, honey or jar). The teacher must name every picture for the whole class, not only for the child who asks.

instruction.now: Write the letter that each picture begins with.
instruction.better: I will say the name of each picture. Write the letter for the sound you hear at the beginning.
instruction.why: A picture does not begin with a letter, a word does; and jar, deer and tie all have other names (glass, fawn, necktie).

instruction.now: Write the letter that each picture ends with.
instruction.better: I will say the name of each picture. Write the letter for the sound you hear at the end.
instruction.why: Same reason; the pen can be taken for a pencil (ends in l) or a crayon, and the shorts for pants.

instruction.now: Say the picture word slowly. Draw one dot in the long box for every sound you hear. Then write how many sounds in the small box.
instruction.better: I will say the name of each picture. Say the word slowly. Draw one dot in the long box for every sound you hear. Then write the number of sounds in the small box.
instruction.why: The count depends on the word, so the teacher names it; 'write how many sounds' is not a full sentence for a child.

instruction.now: Say the word slowly. Write one sound in each box, starting from the left. Leave the boxes you do not need empty.
instruction.better: Say the picture word slowly. Write the letter or letters for each sound in its own box. Start at the left. Leave the boxes you do not need empty.
instruction.why: Children write letters, not sounds; 'the letter or letters' tells them that sh goes in one box.

instruction.now: No word bank this time. Write each picture word on the lines.
instruction.better: Write the word for each picture on the lines.
instruction.why: 'No word bank this time' points back to an earlier worksheet page; on the check it means nothing.

instruction.now: Look at each shape, even the turned and skinny ones, and circle its name.
instruction.better: Look at each shape. Some are turned and some are skinny. I will read the three names. Circle the name of the shape.
instruction.why: Most Kindergartners cannot read 'rectangle' or 'triangle'; the teacher has to read the choices, or the part checks reading and not shapes.

instruction.now: Circle the picture that shows the mirror image.
instruction.better: Look at the first picture. Then look at the three pictures after the dotted line. Circle the one that shows the first picture in a mirror.
instruction.why: 'The mirror image' of what? A Kindergartner needs to be told which picture is the model and where the choices are.

instruction.now: Read the name in each row and circle every shape that really is that shape.
instruction.better: Read the name. Circle every shape that really is that shape.
instruction.why: The check has only one row.

instruction.now: Ring groups of the second number in each pile. Write how many groups you made and how many pictures are left over.
instruction.better: Circle equal groups in the pile. The second number tells you how many go in each group. Write how many groups you made and how many pictures are left over.
instruction.why: US classrooms say 'circle', not 'ring'; 'groups of the second number' is hard to follow, and there is only one pile.

instruction.now: Share the pile equally into the bins. Write how many each gets.
instruction.better: Share the pile equally among the bins. Write how many each bin gets.
instruction.why: Small wording fix; 'each' needs its noun for third graders.

checks.why: Parts 3 and 5 are sound; part 4 is above Kindergarten and parts 1 and 2 each have a picture with the wrong name; without a rhyme part it is still a fair check once the teacher names every picture.

The syllable part is fine, but the sound boxes and the spelling part use words that are not spelled the way they sound; with regular words the three parts are a fair check, though rhyme and word families are not checked at all.
Parts 1 and 3 are right and have one answer each; only the word 'vulture' and the misleading small pictures in part 2 must change; the three parts are a fair check of the unit.

Pronouns, synonyms and root words are right; the opposites part has one box far too hard in A and one box with two defensible answers in B; half of the eight lessons (ABC order, word classes, a/an, shades of meaning) are not checked, which the teacher should be told.

All answers are right, but the key of part 2 shows no lines, part 3 needs a second accepted answer, and part 1 labels only one of four pictures; a fair check of three of the six lessons, a little easy for Grade 2.
Every lesson has a part and every keyed answer is right, but in parts 2, 3 and 4 the two forms are not at the same level and the fox mirror picture cannot be judged by a five-year-old.

The three parts are right once the key of part 3 is redrawn, but they are NOT a fair check of the unit: nothing on sorting, picture graphs or bar graphs, which are four of the seven lessons and a third of the title; add a graph part or say on the teacher page that graphs are not checked.

All six sums are right, but every one is two-digit without regrouping, nothing goes above 100 and nothing is subtracted vertically, so a child can get full marks without the main skills of the unit; it is a fair check only after part 3 gains a subtraction and a regrouping box.
All answers are right and the three parts cover sharing, missing factor and remainders fairly; only the 5 x 5 box and two direction lines need to change.
The new part 2 is right in all four boxes (14 = 7 pairs even, 11 = 5 pairs odd, 17 = 8 pairs odd, 12 = 6 pairs even), A and B match in size and the odd/even order differs between the forms.
The new part 1 is right in all four boxes, but Check A (5 and a 14 printed as two rows of 7) is much easier than Check B (13 and 18).

notes: Answer keys: several drawn answers are not shown in orange or are missing, so a teacher cannot read the key and I could not tell the key from the child's page: lines in G2 grammar part 2 and G1 shapes part 3 (missing), digits in G2 add-subtract part 3 (missing), tangram lines in K shapes part 3, syllable scoops in G1 sounds part 3 and the shaded unit squares in G1 shapes part 2 (all green). Please confirm that none of the green answers is printed on the child's page; if the scoops or the shaded squares are, those parts give the answer away.

G1 sounds part 1: say in the key how to score the spelling of a sound (wolf written w-u-l-f has all four sounds). My advice: one point when each box holds one sound in the right order, whatever the spelling.

G1 sounds part 3: Check A box 1 is a 2-syllable word (rabbit), Check B box 1 a 3-syllable word (strawberry); box 2 is a 1-syllable word in both forms. Better: one 2-syllable and one 3-syllable word in each form.
G1 reading part 2 and G2 grammar part 3: the words to look at are marked with a pale highlight. On a black-and-white copy it may vanish. Underline them and say 'Look at the underlined words.'

G1 words part 3: 'cheerful' is in both boxes of Check A, and 'strong' and 'surprised' are in both boxes of Check B (each is the answer in one box and a wrong choice in the other). Use different wrong choices. gloomy, astonished, powerful and cheerful are hard to read in Grade 1; tell the teacher she may read the four words aloud.
The word 'vulture' is in two checks (G1 reading part 2, G2 grammar part 3). It looks like a stock noun of the worksheet; use animals children can read: cat, dog, hen, duck, frog.

K shapes part 1: Check A (circle, thin triangle) is a little easier than Check B (turned square, turned rectangle with 'square' as a choice). Better: one easy and one turned four-sided shape in each form.

G2 grammar part 1: all four plurals only add -s (hens, ducks, bats, balls), which is Grade 1 work. For Grade 2 one box per form should need -es or a changed word (foxes, boxes, mice, feet), if the lesson teaches them.

G3 division part 3: in both keys the letter R between the two answer boxes is partly covered by the orange outline (it reads like an F). Check that the R is whole on the child's page. Both forms have a remainder of 1; give one form a different remainder.

K hearing: the key prints capital letters in part 2 and small letters in part 3; say in the key that either is right. In part 5 all three words of Check A have a in the middle (bat, bag, cap), Check B has cup; swap one A word for a word with another vowel (pig, sun).

K hearing part 3: lamp, scarf, shorts and sink end in two consonants; they are fine for the last sound, but pen and bed are the right Kindergarten level. If the worksheet has more CVC pictures (bus, dog, cat, sun), use them.
G1 reading part 1: Check A is a five-word statement, Check B a four-word question. Both have one answer; acceptable, but two statements or two questions of the same length would match better.
G2 add-subtract parts 1 and 2: the answers of A and B are almost the same (76 and 78, 36 and 37). It is not an error, but the two forms should not look alike to a child who took Check A.

G1 doubles part 2 and G2 equal groups part 1: odd and even is a Grade 2 standard (2.OA.C.3); in the Grade 1 check it is fine only as long as the unit really teaches it, and 17 pictures is the most a first grader should have to pair.
Coverage the teacher page should state: K hearing has no rhyme part; G1 sounds has no rhyme, word-family or sh/ch/th part; G1 shapes has no graph or sorting part; G3 division has no word problem.
